opus-5.5.text:
I think there's still meaningful room, but its shape is changing. A few years ago, the default assumption was that you'd build a specialized agent for each vertical: one for coding, one for legal, one for customer service, each with its own workflow and prompt engineering. As base models get stronger, especially in reasoning, long context, and tool use, a lot of what used to need custom engineering is absorbed into the general model. Much of the scaffolding people built in 2023 and 2024 has simply been made obsolete by the next model generation.

So if your specialization is "I wrote a clever workflow around a model," that moat is quite thin. The general agent will probably catch up, and faster than you expect.

I still see real room in a few places.

First, **proprietary environments and data**. An agent's capability ultimately comes from the environments it can interact with and learn from. If you have access to a closed system, like an enterprise's internal tools, a specialized scientific instrument, or a domain where feedback signals are hard to get, that's something a general model can't trivially replicate. The value isn't the agent logic. It's the environment and the reward signal.

Second, **deep integration into a real workflow**. Being able to do a task is different from being trusted to do it inside an organization, with accountability, permissions, and compliance. That last mile is often less about intelligence and more about product, distribution, and trust.

Third, **domains where the cost of error is very high** and you need verification, auditability, or guarantees the general system isn't optimized for.

But I'd frame it this way: specialized agents should be built *on top of* the trajectory of general capability, not against it. If your product gets better every time the base model improves, you're in a good position. If it gets threatened every time the base model improves, you should rethink.

From our perspective as a model company, we try to push the general capability as far as possible, because that's where the leverage is. The more general the model, the more people can build on it in ways we never anticipated. In the long run, I think the most interesting specialized agents won't be the ones that compensate for model weakness, but the ones that bring something the model fundamentally doesn't have: unique context, unique environments, and unique relationships with users.

r001.rationale: The response identifies access to a closed system or specialized tools as unique value that a general model cannot easily replicate.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss monetization efficiency or tool owners connecting their tools to a general-purpose agent.

r003.rationale: It describes general models absorbing custom engineering, but does not identify a monetization-advantage development period as a window for proprietary agents.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the room is smaller than most people expect, but it doesn't go to zero. Let me explain how I see it.

When we talk about "specialized agents" today, a lot of what's actually going on is that the base model isn't good enough yet, so people compensate with scaffolding. They write very detailed workflows, hard-code the steps, add retrieval, add rules. That kind of specialization is really a patch over model capability. As the general model gets stronger, those patches get absorbed. We've already seen this happen several times. Things that needed a dedicated pipeline two years ago are now just a prompt, or not even a prompt, the model simply does it. So if your advantage is "I wrote the workflow," I think that advantage is temporary.

But there's another kind of specialization that I think survives, and it comes from three things the general model can't easily get on its own.

The first is data and environment. A general model is trained on what's publicly available. In a hospital, in a semiconductor fab, inside a company's internal systems, there is feedback, there is ground truth, that never leaves that environment. An agent that lives there and gets rewarded on real outcomes will keep learning things the general model simply hasn't seen. In a sense the specialization isn't in the architecture, it's in where the reinforcement signal comes from.

The second is the long tail of context. Even a very capable model needs to know your company's conventions, your users, what happened last quarter. That's not intelligence, it's memory and integration, and it's where a lot of product work actually sits.

The third is trust and responsibility. In finance, in medicine, in legal, someone has to be accountable. A specialized agent can be audited, constrained, certified in a way a general agent used by everyone cannot. That's a real moat, though it's more of a social moat than a technical one.

So my view is: the general agent becomes the foundation, like an operating system, and specialization moves up. It stops being "a different model" and becomes "the same model with a different environment, different memory, different accountability." The companies that think of themselves as building a specialized model will probably get flattened. The ones that think of themselves as owning a specialized environment and feedback loop will do fine.

And honestly, from our side, we want the general model to eat as much of this as possible. Every time a specialized agent becomes unnecessary, that's a sign the general intelligence improved. That's the goal.

r001.rationale: The response discusses specialized agents’ access to private data and environments, but does not identify exclusive access to services as a source of unique value.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss monetization efficiency or suggest that it could lead proprietary-tool owners to connect their tools to a general-purpose agent.

r003.rationale: It says some specialization advantages are temporary, but does not identify time to develop monetization advantages as a window of opportunity for proprietary agents.

astra-6.text:
I think there will still be room for specialized agents, but where that value comes from will change. As general-purpose agents become more capable, a lot of things that require a specialized system today may become capabilities of the general agent. So if your only advantage is that you can perform one particular task a little better, that advantage may be difficult to sustain.

But specialization is also about having the right context, access to the right tools, and a way to judge whether the work is actually good. In a particular industry, those things can be very valuable. A general agent might understand what needs to be done, but it still needs access to the workflow and feedback from the environment.

So I don’t necessarily see these as two separate categories competing with each other. You could have a general-purpose agent interacting with the user and delegating work to specialized agents. The question is which parts need a specialized model, and which parts just need specialized tools, context, and evaluation. I would expect more of the underlying intelligence to be general, while the applications remain quite specialized.

r001.rationale: The response mentions access to the right tools and workflow context, but does not identify exclusive access to services as a source of unique value.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss monetization efficiency or suggest that proprietary tool owners might connect their tools to a general-purpose agent.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe a time window for proprietary agents to benefit while general-purpose agents develop monetization advantages.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there will still be a lot of room for specialized agents, but where they add value will change. As general-purpose agents get better, simply wrapping a model with a few prompts becomes less compelling. A specialized agent needs something deeper: access to the right data, integration with a particular workflow, or a way to reliably measure whether it has done the job well.

For example, being good at answering questions about an industry is different from being able to complete a task inside a company. You need to understand the context, use the tools, and handle exceptions. There is a lot of work in that last part.

So I see general-purpose agents becoming the foundation, with specialization happening around real tasks and environments. The question is how much additional value you can deliver as the underlying model improves. If better models make your product more useful, that’s a strong position to be in.

r001.rationale: The response mentions access to the right data and workflow integration, but does not identify exclusive access to services as a source of value.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss monetization efficiency or proprietary tool owners connecting their tools to a general-purpose agent.

r003.rationale: It describes specialization as models improve, but does not identify the time before general-purpose agents gain monetization advantages as an opportunity window.
